quiz.q:
Punch work and the mean-power argument

Problem. A press punches a 20 mm hole in 10 mm plate of ultimate shear strength 350 MPa, at 30 strokes per minute. Find the peak punch force, the work per stroke, and the mean power. If the punch occupies 15% of the crank cycle, find the peak and mean torques and hence the power a motor would need with no flywheel fitted, at a shaft speed of 360 rev/min.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) The sheared area is the hole circumference times the plate thickness: \( A = \pi d t = \pi(0.020)(0.010) = 6.283\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2} \), so \( F = A\tau = 6.283\times10^{-4}(350\times10^6) = 219\,911\ \mathrm{N} \).

(2) The force rises to that peak and falls as the slug shears, so the work is about \( \tfrac12 F t = \tfrac12(219\,911)(0.010) = 1100\ \mathrm{J} \).

(3) Mean power \( = 1100(30)/60 = 550\ \mathrm{W} \).

(4) Mean torque \( = W/2\pi = 1100/6.2832 = 175.0\ \mathrm{N\cdot m} \); punch torque \( = W/(0.15\times2\pi) = 1100/0.9425 = 1166.7\ \mathrm{N\cdot m} \).

(5) The crank turns at 30 rev/min, so \( \omega = 2\pi(30)/60 = 3.1416\ \mathrm{rad/s} \) and a motor meeting the peak directly needs \( 1166.7(3.1416) = 3665\ \mathrm{W} = 3.67\ \mathrm{kW} \).

Answer: 219.9 kN, 1100 J, 550 W mean; 175.0 and 1166.7 N·m; 3.67 kW without a flywheel. Sanity check: \( 3665/550 = 6.67 \), exactly \( T_{\text{punch}}/T_{\text{mean}} = 1166.7/175.0 \), as it must be since both powers are taken at the same shaft speed — so the flywheel's job is to let the motor be sized for the smaller of the two. Note also that the sheared area is the hole circumference times the thickness: using \( \pi d^2/4 \) would have given 110 kN, 2.5 times too small, and it is the commonest error in this calculation.

quiz.q:
Sizing the flywheel

Problem. For the press above, find the energy fluctuation \( \Delta E \), then the flywheel inertia needed for \( C_s = 0.02 \) with the flywheel on the motor-side shaft at 360 rev/min, the rim mass if the rim sits at 0.6 m radius, and the resulting maximum and minimum angular speeds. Compare with fitting it to the 30 rev/min crank shaft instead.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) The flywheel supplies whatever the punch demands above the mean: \( \Delta E = (1166.7-175.0)(0.15\times2\pi) = 991.7(0.9425) = 934.6\ \mathrm{J} \). Equivalently \( \Delta E = W(1-0.15) = 1100(0.85) = 935\ \mathrm{J} \).

(2) \( \omega = 37.699\ \mathrm{rad/s} \), so \( I = \dfrac{\Delta E}{C_s\omega^2} = \dfrac{934.6}{0.02(1421.2)} = \dfrac{934.6}{28.42} = 32.88\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2} \).

(3) Treating the rim as carrying it all, \( m = I/r^2 = 32.88/0.36 = 91.3\ \mathrm{kg} \).

(4) \( \omega_{\max} = \omega(1+C_s/2) = 38.08 \) and \( \omega_{\min} = \omega(1-C_s/2) = 37.32\ \mathrm{rad/s} \).

(5) On the crank shaft, \( \omega = 3.1416\ \mathrm{rad/s} \) and \( I = 934.6/(0.02\times9.870) = 4735\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2} \) — 144 times as much for the same duty, which is \( 12^2 \).

Answer: \( \Delta E = 935 \) J, \( I = 32.9\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2} \), rim about 91 kg, speed between 37.32 and 38.08 rad/s; 4735 kg·m² if fitted to the crank. Sanity check: \( (\omega_{\max}-\omega_{\min})/\omega = 0.756/37.70 = 0.0200 \) ✓ — the specification recovered from the answer. The two routes to \( \Delta E \) also agree, and the second is worth remembering: the flywheel supplies the whole punch work less the fraction the motor contributes during the punch itself.

quiz.q:
What tightening \( C_s \) and changing shaft speed cost

Problem. Using \( \Delta E = 934.6 \) J, find the flywheel inertia needed if \( C_s \) is tightened from 0.02 to 0.005 at the same 360 rev/min, and the inertia needed at \( C_s = 0.02 \) if the flywheel is moved to a shaft running at 720 rev/min. State the design rule that follows.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Tightening \( C_s \): \( I = \dfrac{934.6}{0.005(37.699)^2} = \dfrac{934.6}{7.106} = 131.5\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2} \) — exactly four times the original 32.88, since \( I \propto 1/C_s \) and \( C_s \) was quartered.

(2) Doubling the speed: \( \omega = 75.398\ \mathrm{rad/s} \), so \( I = \dfrac{934.6}{0.02(5684.9)} = 8.22\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2} \) — a quarter of the original, since \( I\propto1/\omega^2 \).

(3) Rule: fit the flywheel to the fastest shaft that carries the fluctuation, and specify the loosest \( C_s \) the process will accept.

Answer: 131.5 kg·m² at \( C_s=0.005 \); 8.22 kg·m² at 720 rev/min; both follow from the inverse dependences in \( I=\Delta E/(C_s\omega^2) \). Sanity check: the two effects together span a factor of sixteen in inertia for the same job, which is why flywheel decisions are made before the layout is fixed rather than after. The speed rule has a limit the equation does not show: rim stress goes as \( \rho v^2 \), so a flywheel on a fast shaft approaches its burst speed sooner, and the gyroscopic couple it contributes (Lesson 11) grows with \( \omega \) as well.

quiz.q: On a turning-moment diagram, the area between the curve and the mean-torque line is
choices: the energy the flywheel must absorb or supply
quiz.solution: \( W=\int T\,d\theta \), so an area on a torque-against-angle plot is an energy. Above the mean line the machine is demanding more than the motor supplies and the deficit comes from the flywheel; below it, the motor runs ahead and the flywheel takes the surplus back. The largest accumulated area between two crossings of the mean line is \( \Delta E \).

quiz.q: The coefficient of fluctuation of speed \( C_s \) is defined as
quiz.solution: It is the speed range as a fraction of the mean, and it is a specification chosen from the application rather than a property of the machine. The relation \( \Delta E = I\omega^2C_s \) then follows from the kinetic-energy difference, with \( \omega_{\max}+\omega_{\min} \) approximated as \( 2\omega_{\text{mean}} \) — an approximation good to a fraction of a per cent at any realistic \( C_s \).

quiz.q: A flywheel is sized for \( C_s = 0.02 \). Tightening the requirement to \( C_s = 0.005 \) changes the required inertia by a factor of
quiz.solution: \( I = \Delta E/(C_s\omega^2) \), so \( I \propto 1/C_s \): quartering \( C_s \) quadruples \( I \), from 32.9 to 131.5 kg·m² in the worked press. Smoothness is bought linearly in inertia, and inertia costs mass, start-up time and rim stress — which is why the loosest acceptable \( C_s \) is the right specification.

quiz.q: Moving a flywheel from a shaft at 360 rev/min to one at 720 rev/min, for the same \( \Delta E \) and \( C_s \), changes the required inertia by a factor of
quiz.solution: \( I \propto 1/\omega^2 \), so doubling the speed quarters the inertia — 32.9 kg·m² becomes 8.22. This is the single most effective flywheel decision available, and it is why the wheel goes on the fastest shaft that carries the fluctuation. The limits are rim stress, which goes as \( \rho v^2 \), and the gyroscopic couple the faster wheel contributes.

quiz.q: The distinction between a flywheel and a governor is that
choices: a flywheel controls fluctuation within a cycle; a governor sets the mean speed
they do the same job by different means
quiz.solution: A flywheel is an energy store that limits the swing within one revolution and has no view about what the average speed should be. A governor adjusts the energy supplied to hold the mean where it is wanted and cannot respond within a cycle. A machine with a flywheel and no governor runs smoothly at whatever speed the load dictates; one with a governor and no flywheel holds the right average while surging within each revolution.

quiz.q: Punching a 20 mm hole in 10 mm plate of 350 MPa shear strength requires a peak force of about
quiz.solution: \( F = \pi d t\tau = \pi(0.020)(0.010)(350\times10^6) = 219.9 \) kN. The sheared area is the circumference times the thickness, not the hole's cross-sectional area — using \( \pi d^2/4 \) instead is the standard error and gives a figure 2.5 times too small here. The work per stroke is roughly half the peak force times the thickness, because the force builds and falls as the slug shears.

quiz.q: A press absorbs 1100 J per stroke in 15% of its cycle. The energy the flywheel must handle is
quiz.solution: The motor contributes its mean torque throughout, including during the punch, so the flywheel supplies the rest: \( \Delta E = W(1-0.15) = 935 \) J. Computed the other way, \( (1166.7-175.0)(0.15\times2\pi) = 934.6 \) J — the same number from the area between the pulse and the mean line, which is the check worth doing.

quiz.q: An unnecessarily large flywheel penalises a machine mainly through
choices: longer start-up, higher starting current, rim stress and gyroscopic couple
quiz.solution: Its own inertia must be accelerated at every start, so start times and starting currents rise with it; its rim stress goes as \( \rho v^2 \) toward a burst speed; and it adds a gyroscopic couple to any machine that changes orientation. Mean power is set by the work per cycle and the rate, and is unaffected — the flywheel neither adds nor removes energy over a complete cycle.

9.kuwait:
Applied case — the press that tripped its motor after a die change. A punching press ran for years on a modest motor. A new die was fitted to punch a larger hole in thicker plate, and the press began tripping its motor overload on some strokes and stalling on others. The motor was tested, found sound, and replaced with a larger one, which cured the tripping and introduced a new problem: the drive belts began to fail.

The flywheel had not been reconsidered. Punch work scales as \( \tfrac12(\pi dt\tau)t \) — with the hole diameter and, more strongly, the plate thickness, since thickness enters twice. The original duty of about 1100 J per stroke, with a mean torque of 175 N·m and an energy fluctuation of 935 J, had been matched to a flywheel of roughly 33 kg·m² on the 360 rev/min motor-side shaft for \( C_s = 0.02 \). A larger hole in thicker plate raised \( \Delta E \) proportionally, and since \( C_s = \Delta E/(I\omega^2) \) with \( I \) unchanged, the speed fluctuation rose in step. The shaft was being dragged down far enough during each punch for the motor to see the load as a stall. Fitting a bigger motor treated the symptom: the motor then supplied the peak directly, through the belts, which is exactly the path the flywheel had been installed to avoid, at nearly seven times the mean torque.

Two practices follow. A die change is a change to the turning-moment diagram, so the flywheel calculation is part of the tooling change and not part of the motor's file. And a motor that trips on an intermittent-duty machine is evidence about the energy store before it is evidence about the motor: the useful first check is \( \Delta E \) against \( I\omega^2C_s \), which takes one line.
9.recap:
• A turning-moment diagram plots torque against crank angle; its area is work and its mean height is the motor duty.
  • Punching a 20 mm hole in 10 mm of 350 MPa plate takes \( \pi dt\tau = 219.9 \) kN peak and about \( \tfrac12 Ft = 1100 \) J of work.
  • At 30 strokes/min that is 550 W mean, while the demand during the punch is 1167 N·m — 3.67 kW at the crank, 6.7 times the mean.
  • \( \Delta E \) is the area between the curve and the mean line, here 935 J, equal to \( W(1-0.15) \) — two routes, same number.
  • \( C_s=(\omega_{\max}-\omega_{\min})/\omega_{\text{mean}} \) is a specification: 0.2 for a crusher, 0.02 for machine tools, 0.003 for alternators.
  • \( I = \Delta E/(C_s\omega^2) = 32.9\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2} \) on the 360 rev/min motor-side shaft — about 91 kg of rim at 0.6 m radius, against 4735 kg·m² on the 30 rev/min crank.
  • Tightening \( C_s \) from 0.02 to 0.005 quadruples the inertia to 131.5 kg·m²; inertia buys smoothness linearly.
  • Doubling the shaft speed quarters the inertia to 8.22 kg·m² — fit the wheel to the fastest shaft carrying the fluctuation.
  • A flywheel governs fluctuation within a cycle; a governor sets the mean speed. They are different problems and different devices.
  • Oversizing costs start-up time, starting current, rim stress (\( \sigma\propto\rho v^2 \)) and gyroscopic couple — specify the loosest \( C_s \) the process allows.

10.lecture:
§1 · What unbalance is

A rotor is balanced when its mass is distributed so that rotation produces no net force or couple on the bearings. It almost never is, as machined: a keyway on one side, a core shift in a casting, a coating applied unevenly, a blade replaced with one a few grams heavier. Each leaves an effective mass \( m \) at an effective radius \( r \), and rotation turns that into a force \( m\omega^2 r \) rotating with the shaft — which the bearings feel as a load at once per revolution, forever.

The \( \omega^2 \) is what makes it a running problem rather than a manufacturing curiosity. A 5 g residual at 100 mm on a rotor at 3000 rev/min produces \( 0.005(314.2)^2(0.1) = 49\ \mathrm{N} \) — five kilograms of force from five grams of metal, cycling fifty times a second. Double the speed and it is 197 N.

§2 · One plane or two

If the whole unbalance lies in a single transverse plane — a thin disc, a fan wheel — a single correction mass in that plane cancels it. The condition is that the \( m r \) vectors sum to zero.

A long rotor is not that. Two equal unbalances at opposite ends and 180° apart sum to zero force and still shake the machine: they form a couple that rocks the rotor about its centre, loading one bearing up while the other goes down. Cancelling force alone is not enough, so two conditions must be satisfied at once, and satisfying two vector conditions needs two correction planes.

Key relations — two-plane balancing

\[ \sum m_ir_i=0 \quad\text{(force)},\qquad \sum m_ir_ia_i=0 \quad\text{(couple)} \]

\( a_i \) is the axial distance from a chosen reference plane. Solve the couple equation first — taking moments about one correction plane removes that plane's unknown — then use the force equation for the remaining one.

Work an example. A shaft carries 5 kg at 100 mm and 0°; 8 kg at 80 mm and 120°, 200 mm along; 6 kg at 120 mm and 240°, 400 mm along. Correction planes are at 0 and 600 mm. The \( mr \) products are 500, 640 and 720 kg·mm, and resolving gives \( \sum mr = (-180.0,\ -69.3) \), a residual of 192.9 kg·mm at 201.1°. Taking moments about the left plane and dividing by the 600 mm span gives the right-plane correction as 416.6 kg·mm at 33.7°; putting that back into the force equation gives the left-plane correction as 232.2 kg·mm at 224.1°. At a 100 mm correction radius those are 4.17 kg and 2.32 kg.

Notice that the single-plane answer — 192.9 kg·mm — matches neither correction. A rotor balanced in one plane when it needed two is not partly fixed; it has had its force cancelled and its couple left behind, and it will still shake.

§3 · Reciprocating masses, and the term that cannot be cancelled

Lesson 3 gave the piston acceleration as \( a=-r\omega^2(\cos\theta+\cos2\theta/n) \). Multiply by the reciprocating mass and the shaking force follows directly.

Key relation — single-cylinder shaking force

\[ F=m\omega^2r\cos\theta+\frac{m\omega^2r}{n}\cos2\theta \]

The first term is the primary, at crank frequency; the second is the secondary, at twice crank frequency, with \( 1/n \) of the amplitude.

For \( m=1.5 \) kg, \( r=50 \) mm, \( \omega=150 \) rad/s and \( n=4 \): primary 1687.5 N, secondary 421.9 N, and 2109.4 N combined at top dead centre against 1265.6 N at the bottom. The asymmetry between the two ends is the secondary term, and it exists only because the connecting rod is of finite length.

Here is the difficulty. A rotating unbalance is a rotating vector, and another rotating vector cancels it exactly. A reciprocating force is not a rotating vector — it oscillates along one line. A rotating balance mass can be made to cancel it in that direction, but the same mass then produces an equal force perpendicular to it, which was not there before. Nothing has been removed; the unbalance has been rotated by 90°.

So a single cylinder is partially balanced: cancel a fraction \( c \) of the primary and accept \( c \) of it appearing transversely. The residual peaks at \( \max(c,\,1-c)\,m\omega^2 r \), which is smallest at \( c=\tfrac12 \) — 843.8 N here, half the unbalanced primary, and the best a single cylinder can do. A locomotive practice of \( c=\tfrac23 \) gives 1125 N and reflects a different judgement: it favours the along-track direction at the expense of the vertical hammer-blow on the rail.

The secondary is worse still. No mass rotating at crank speed can produce a force at twice crank speed, so cancelling it requires shafts geared to run at \( 2\omega \), carrying their own weights. Some large engines carry exactly that; most accept the secondary and place it where the structure can take it.

§4 · Multi-cylinder engines and field balancing

What one cylinder cannot do, several can. Arrange cylinders along a crankshaft with chosen crank angles and the primary forces, primary couples, secondary forces and secondary couples can each be made to sum to zero — four conditions, satisfied by geometry rather than by added mass. An inline four with cranks at 0°, 180°, 180°, 0° cancels the primary forces and both couples, but its four secondaries all peak together and add: the residual is four times one cylinder's secondary, at twice crank speed. That is the characteristic four-cylinder vibration, and it is why balance shafts turning at \( 2\omega \) are fitted to larger fours.

Balancing in service reverses the calculation. The unbalance is unknown, so it is measured: run the rotor, record amplitude and phase at each bearing, add a known trial mass, run again, and the change in the vector response gives the influence coefficient linking correction to response. Two planes need a two-by-two influence matrix and two trial runs. The arithmetic is the same \( mr \) vector algebra worked above — the difference is only that the numbers are measured rather than given.

One reading matters diagnostically. Unbalance produces a once-per-revolution response, so a vibration spectrum with a dominant line at running speed points at balance; the gear-mesh lines of Lesson 6 sit far above it; and a strong twice-per-revolution line on a reciprocating machine is the secondary term of this lesson, not a balance fault at all.
10.foundations:
What this lesson assumes

  • Piston acceleration (Lesson 3) — the primary and secondary terms come directly from \( \cos\theta + \cos2\theta/n \).
  • Shaking force (Lesson 7) — what balancing exists to remove.
  • Vector addition and moments (Statics L2) — the two-plane conditions are a force polygon and a moment polygon.
  • Centripetal force (Dynamics L3) — \( m\omega^2r \), the whole rotating-unbalance mechanism.
  • Frequency in a spectrum (Lesson 6) — distinguishing a once-per-revolution balance line from a mesh line.

quiz.q:
Two-plane balancing of a shaft

Problem. A shaft carries 5 kg at 100 mm radius and 0°, at axial station 0; 8 kg at 80 mm and 120°, at 200 mm; and 6 kg at 120 mm and 240°, at 400 mm. Correction planes are available at 0 and 600 mm. Find both correction \( mr \) products and their angles, and the masses required at a 100 mm radius.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) The \( mr \) products are 500, 640 and 720 kg·mm. Resolving:

\( \sum mr\cos = 500 + 640\cos120^\circ + 720\cos240^\circ = 500-320-360 = -180.0 \);
\( \sum mr\sin = 0 + 640\sin120^\circ + 720\sin240^\circ = 554.26-623.54 = -69.28 \) kg·mm.

(2) Moments about the left plane (station 0), so its correction drops out:

\( \sum mra\cos = 0(500) + 200(-320) + 400(-360) = -208\,000 \);
\( \sum mra\sin = 0 + 200(554.26) + 400(-623.54) = -138\,564 \) kg·mm².

(3) The right-plane correction at 600 mm must cancel those: \( (m_Rr_R)_x = 208\,000/600 = 346.67 \), \( (m_Rr_R)_y = 138\,564/600 = 230.94 \), so \( m_Rr_R = \sqrt{346.67^2+230.94^2} = 416.6 \) kg·mm at \( \arctan(230.94/346.67) = 33.67^\circ \).

(4) Force equation for the left plane: \( (m_Lr_L)_x = -(-180.0+346.67) = -166.67 \), \( (m_Lr_L)_y = -(-69.28+230.94) = -161.66 \), giving 232.2 kg·mm at 224.13°.

(5) At 100 mm radius: 4.17 kg in the right plane and 2.32 kg in the left.

Answer: 416.6 kg·mm at 33.67° (4.17 kg) and 232.2 kg·mm at 224.13° (2.32 kg). Sanity check: substituting both corrections back gives \( \sum mr = 0 \) and \( \sum mra = 0 \) to machine precision — both conditions, which is the test that the couple was not forgotten. Note that a single-plane treatment would have called for 192.9 kg·mm at 201.1°, which is neither of the correct answers: it cancels the force and leaves the couple, so the rotor would still rock its bearings.

quiz.q:
Primary and secondary shaking force

Problem. A single cylinder has 1.5 kg of reciprocating mass, a 50 mm crank, a rod ratio \( n = 4 \), and runs at 150 rad/s. Find the primary and secondary force amplitudes and the total shaking force at top dead centre and at bottom dead centre.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( m\omega^2r = 1.5(150)^2(0.050) = 1.5(22\,500)(0.050) = 1687.5\ \mathrm{N} \) — the primary amplitude.

(2) Secondary amplitude \( = 1687.5/n = 1687.5/4 = 421.9\ \mathrm{N} \).

(3) At \( \theta = 0 \): \( \cos0 = 1 \) and \( \cos0 = 1 \), so \( F = 1687.5 + 421.9 = 2109.4\ \mathrm{N} \).

(4) At \( \theta = 180^\circ \): \( \cos180^\circ = -1 \) and \( \cos360^\circ = +1 \), so \( F = -1687.5 + 421.9 = -1265.6\ \mathrm{N} \).

Answer: 1687.5 N and 421.9 N; 2109.4 N at top dead centre and 1265.6 N at bottom. Sanity check: the two dead centres differ by 843.8 N, which is exactly twice the secondary amplitude — the primary reverses cleanly while the secondary returns to the same sign, since it goes through two full cycles per revolution. That asymmetry is a direct consequence of the connecting rod's finite length, and it is the reason the top of the stroke governs. An infinitely long rod would give \( \pm1687.5 \) N and nothing else.

quiz.q:
Partial balance: choosing the fraction (with a US customary check)

Problem. For the cylinder above, a rotating balance mass cancels a fraction \( c \) of the primary force but introduces the same fraction transversely. Find the peak residual force for \( c = 0 \), \( c = \tfrac12 \) and \( c = \tfrac23 \), state which is best and why the other is used, and give the best value in pounds-force.
quiz.solution:
Solution. Along the cylinder axis the residual primary is \( (1-c)m\omega^2r \); perpendicular to it the introduced force is \( c\,m\omega^2 r \). Over a revolution the resultant traces an ellipse whose largest value is \( \max(c,\,1-c)\,m\omega^2r \).

(1) \( c=0 \): \( \max(0,1)(1687.5) = 1687.5\ \mathrm{N} \) — the whole primary, along the cylinder axis.

(2) \( c=\tfrac12 \): \( \max(0.5,0.5)(1687.5) = 843.8\ \mathrm{N} \).

(3) \( c=\tfrac23 \): \( \max(0.667,0.333)(1687.5) = 1125.0\ \mathrm{N} \), now transverse rather than axial.

(4) \( 843.8\ \mathrm{N} \div 4.448 = 189.7\ \mathrm{lbf} \).

Answer: 1687.5, 843.8 and 1125.0 N; \( c=\tfrac12 \) minimises the peak at 843.8 N (189.7 lbf), half the unbalanced primary. Sanity check: the minimum of \( \max(c,1-c) \) is at \( c=\tfrac12 \) by inspection, so the result needs no calculus and holds for any engine. The reason \( c=\tfrac23 \) survives in locomotive practice is that the two directions are not equally acceptable there: a vertical force lifts the wheel off the rail (hammer blow) while a longitudinal one merely surges the train, so the larger residual is deliberately placed where it does least harm. "Best" depends on which direction the structure can take.

quiz.q: A rotating unbalance produces a bearing force that grows as
quiz.solution: \( F = m\omega^2 r \). That square is why a residual unbalance which is harmless on a test stand becomes serious at running speed, and why balancing tolerances are quoted against a service speed rather than absolutely. A 5 g residual at 100 mm gives 49 N at 3000 rev/min and 197 N at 6000.

quiz.q: Two equal unbalances at opposite ends of a rotor, 180° apart, give \( \sum mr = 0 \). The rotor
choices: is balanced for force but not for couple, and will still rock its bearings
needs a larger correction mass in one plane
quiz.solution: The forces cancel and the moments do not: the pair forms a couple that loads one bearing up as the other goes down, once per revolution. This is the standard demonstration that \( \sum mr = 0 \) is necessary and not sufficient, and the reason a long rotor needs two correction planes — two vector conditions require two planes to satisfy them.

quiz.q: In a two-plane balance calculation, moments are taken about one correction plane so as to
choices: eliminate that plane's unknown from the moment equation
make the answer independent of speed
quiz.solution: A correction in the reference plane has zero moment arm about that plane, so it drops out and the moment equation contains only one unknown, which then solves directly. The force equation afterwards yields the second. Speed never appears — \( \omega^2 \) is common to every term and cancels — and the axial positions are essential, not avoidable.

quiz.q: The secondary shaking force of a single cylinder acts at
choices: the natural frequency of the mounting
quiz.solution: It is the \( \cos2\theta \) term, so it completes two cycles per crankshaft revolution, with an amplitude \( 1/n \) of the primary — 421.9 N against 1687.5 N at \( n=4 \). It exists only because the connecting rod has finite length, and it is why a reciprocating machine shows a strong line at twice running speed that has nothing to do with a balance fault.

quiz.q: A rotating mass cannot fully balance a reciprocating mass because
choices: it would have to be too heavy
cancelling the force along the cylinder axis introduces an equal force perpendicular to it
quiz.solution: A rotating unbalance is a rotating vector; a reciprocating force oscillates along one line. A rotating mass matched to cancel the axial component necessarily produces an equal transverse component that was not there before, so the unbalance is rotated rather than removed. That is why single-cylinder practice is partial balance, and why the residual cannot be driven below half the primary.

quiz.q: Balancing a fraction \( c \) of the primary force minimises the peak residual at
quiz.solution: The peak resultant over a revolution is \( \max(c,1-c)m\omega^2r \), which is smallest where the two branches cross, at \( c=\tfrac12 \) — 843.8 N in the worked case, half the unbalanced primary. Locomotive practice used \( \tfrac23 \), giving a larger 1125 N residual placed deliberately in the direction the track could better tolerate; "best" depends on which direction the structure can accept.

quiz.q: An inline four-cylinder engine with cranks at 0°, 180°, 180°, 0° has
choices: no shaking force of any kind
primary forces and couples balanced, but four secondaries that add
quiz.solution: The crank arrangement cancels the primary forces and both couples by geometry, but every cylinder's \( \cos2\theta \) term peaks at the same instant, so the four secondaries add to four times one cylinder's value at twice crank speed. That residual is the characteristic four-cylinder vibration and the reason larger fours are fitted with balance shafts geared to run at \( 2\omega \).

quiz.q: Field balancing determines the required correction by
choices: measuring amplitude and phase, adding a trial mass, and re-measuring
running at several speeds and extrapolating
quiz.solution: The unbalance is unknown in service, so the response to a known trial mass is measured and the influence coefficient — response per unit correction, in amplitude and phase — is deduced from the change. Two planes need two trial runs and a two-by-two matrix. The vector algebra is identical to the worked \( mr \) problem; only the source of the numbers differs.

10.kuwait:
Applied case — the fan that was balanced twice and still shook. A large double-inlet fan was rebalanced after a blade repair. The technician worked in the plane he could reach, added a correction, and got the vibration at the drive-end bearing down to an acceptable figure. The non-drive-end bearing was worse afterwards than before, and within weeks its housing had cracked.

The unbalance was distributed along a wide rotor, so it had both a force and a couple component, and a single-plane correction can only address the force. Cancelling \( \sum mr \) while leaving \( \sum mra \) untouched leaves a pure couple, which rocks the rotor about its centre: one bearing improves and the other necessarily deteriorates. The worked example in this lesson shows the trap numerically — the single-plane answer, 192.9 kg·mm at 201.1°, is neither of the correct two-plane corrections of 416.6 at 33.7° and 232.2 at 224.1°, and applying it alone would have left a substantial couple behind.

Two practices follow. Whether a rotor needs one plane or two is decided by its geometry and its speed, not by which plane is accessible — a wide rotor is a two-plane job and a single-plane correction on one is not a partial fix but a different fault. And balancing is judged at every bearing, not the one being worked on: a correction that improves one measurement while worsening another is the signature of a couple, and it is telling the technician which calculation was skipped.
10.recap:
• Unbalance is an effective \( mr \) that rotation turns into \( m\omega^2r \) — a once-per-revolution bearing load whose size goes as the square of speed.
  • Single-plane balance requires \( \sum m_ir_i=0 \); that is necessary and not sufficient for a long rotor.
  • Two equal unbalances 180° apart at opposite ends sum to zero force and leave a couple that rocks the bearings — hence two conditions and two correction planes.
  • \( \sum m_ir_ia_i=0 \) is solved first, about one correction plane, which removes that plane's unknown.
  • The worked shaft needs 416.6 kg·mm at 33.67° and 232.2 kg·mm at 224.13° — 4.17 kg and 2.32 kg at 100 mm radius.
  • Its single-plane answer, 192.9 kg·mm at 201.1°, is neither correction: a one-plane fix on a two-plane rotor cancels force and leaves couple.
  • Reciprocating force is \( m\omega^2r\cos\theta + (m\omega^2r/n)\cos2\theta \) — 1687.5 N primary and 421.9 N secondary here, 2109.4 N at top dead centre against 1265.6 N at bottom.
  • A rotating mass rotates a reciprocating unbalance rather than removing it: cancelling \( c \) of the primary introduces \( c \) transversely.
  • The peak residual is \( \max(c,1-c)m\omega^2r \), minimised at \( c=\tfrac12 \) — 843.8 N, half the primary; locomotive practice used \( \tfrac23 \) to steer the residual into a tolerable direction.
  • An inline four cancels primaries and couples by crank geometry and adds four secondaries at twice crank speed — the reason balance shafts run at \( 2\omega \).
  • Field balancing measures amplitude and phase, adds a trial mass and re-measures; the influence coefficient does the rest, on the same vector algebra.

11.lecture:
§1 · The problem a flywheel cannot solve

Lesson 9 sized a flywheel to hold the speed steady within a cycle. It said nothing about what the average speed should be, and it cannot: a flywheel is a passive store, and if the load falls away it simply carries on turning faster. Holding the mean speed against a changing load is a control problem, and the governor is that controller, built from iron a century before anyone wrote down a transfer function.

The principle is a feedback loop with no electronics in it. Two balls are carried on arms from a spindle driven by the engine. Rotation throws them outward against gravity; the arms lift a sleeve; the sleeve moves a linkage that closes the fuel or steam valve. Speed rises, balls rise, supply falls, speed falls. The equilibrium of the balls is the measurement, and the sleeve position is the control action.

§2 · The Watt governor, and the inverse square that defeats it

Take the simplest arrangement: two balls of mass \( m \) on arms pivoted on the spindle axis, with nothing else attached. Each ball travels a circle of radius \( r \) at angular speed \( \omega \), so the arm must supply a centripetal force \( m\omega^2r \) horizontally and carry the weight \( mg \) vertically. The arm can only pull along its own length, so the ratio of those two components fixes the arm's angle — and with it the height \( h \) of the ball below the pivot.

Key relation — Watt governor height

\[ \tan\theta=\frac{m\omega^2r}{mg}=\frac{r}{h} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad h=\frac{g}{\omega^2}=\frac{895}{N^2}\ \text{metres} \]

with \( N \) in rev/min. The ball mass cancels completely: a heavier ball does not change the height, because it adds to both the centripetal requirement and the weight.

That cancellation is the first surprise and the inverse square is the second. At 60 rev/min, \( h = 0.248 \) m — a governor a quarter of a metre tall, which is workable. At 120 it is 0.062 m, and at 200 it is 0.022 m. The whole travel available to move a valve has shrunk to 22 mm, and the change in that travel for a small speed change is smaller still. Below a certain size the friction in the linkage swamps the signal and the governor stops responding at all.

So the simple Watt governor is a low-speed device, and that is a geometric fact rather than a manufacturing limitation. Every practical governor is a way of defeating it.

§3 · Loading the governor, and the three words that grade it

The Porter governor adds a dead weight \( M \) on the sleeve. The arms now carry the balls' weight and lift the sleeve load, so a much higher rotational speed is needed to reach any given angle — equivalently, at a given speed the balls sit far higher than they would unloaded.

Key relation — Porter governor height

\[ h=\frac{m+M}{m}\cdot\frac{g}{\omega^2} \]

for the arrangement whose upper and lower arms meet on the axis. The factor \( (m+M)/m \) is the design lever, and unlike the Watt case the ball mass now matters.

With a 2 kg ball and a 20 kg sleeve the factor is 11, so the 22 mm of the Watt governor at 200 rev/min becomes 246 mm — usable again. Springs are used the same way in high-speed governors, where the dead weight would be impractically large and its own inertia would make the governor sluggish.

Three properties grade the result. Sensitiveness is the ratio of mean speed to the speed range between the sleeve's extreme positions: a sensitive governor makes a large sleeve movement for a small speed change. Stability requires that each speed correspond to exactly one radius, so the governor settles rather than wanders. And a governor is isochronous when the sleeve moves through its whole travel with no speed change at all — the limiting case of sensitiveness, and a trap: an isochronous governor has no unique equilibrium, so it drives the sleeve hard to one end or the other and the engine hunts, oscillating about the set speed instead of holding it. The cure is deliberate insensitivity plus friction or damping, which is the same conclusion a control engineer reaches about excessive proportional gain, in different words.

§4 · Gyroscopic couples: the reaction to turning a spinning rotor

The last topic of the course is one every rotating machine carries and few analyses include. A spinning rotor has angular momentum \( I\omega \) along its axis. Turn that axis — precess it — and the direction of the momentum vector changes, which requires a torque, and the rotor applies the reaction of that torque to its bearings.

Key relation — gyroscopic couple

\[ C=I\,\omega\,\omega_p \]

\( \omega \) is the spin speed and \( \omega_p \) the precession rate. The couple acts about the axis perpendicular to both, so a rotor precessed in yaw reacts in pitch.

The numbers are not small. A turbine rotor of \( I = 25\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2} \) at 3000 rev/min has \( \omega = 314.2 \) rad/s. Put it in a ship turning at a leisurely 0.1 rad/s and \( C = 25(314.2)(0.1) = 785\ \mathrm{N\cdot m} \). Carried by bearings 2 m apart, that is 393 N up on one and 393 N down on the other — a load that appears only while the vessel turns, reverses when it turns the other way, and is invisible to any analysis done with the ship on a straight course.

The same term explains behaviour that looks like magic elsewhere: a ship's turbine pitching the hull as it turns, a rotor whirling in its clearance, a large flywheel making a vehicle reluctant to change direction. It is also why the flywheel of Lesson 9 is not free — adding inertia to smooth a cycle adds gyroscopic couple to every manoeuvre. Governors and gyroscopes are usually filed as legacy topics; they are better understood as the two places where this course's kinematics reaches directly into how a machine behaves in service.

quiz.q:
The Watt governor's collapse with speed

Problem. Find the ball height of a simple Watt governor at 60, 120 and 200 rev/min. State what happens to the height when the speed doubles, and say why the device is unusable at the highest of the three speeds.
quiz.solution:
Solution. \( h = g/\omega^2 \) with \( \omega = 2\pi N/60 \).

(1) \( N = 60 \): \( \omega = 6.283\ \mathrm{rad/s} \), \( \omega^2 = 39.48 \), so \( h = 9.81/39.48 = 0.2485\ \mathrm{m} \).

(2) \( N = 120 \): \( \omega = 12.566 \), \( \omega^2 = 157.9 \), so \( h = 0.0621\ \mathrm{m} \).

(3) \( N = 200 \): \( \omega = 20.944 \), \( \omega^2 = 438.6 \), so \( h = 0.0224\ \mathrm{m} \).

(4) Doubling the speed quarters the height, since \( h \propto 1/\omega^2 \): 0.2485 to 0.0621 m from 60 to 120 rev/min is a factor of exactly 4.

Answer: 248.5, 62.1 and 22.4 mm; the height falls as the inverse square of speed, and 22 mm is too small to work with. Sanity check: the shortcut \( h = 895/N^2 \) metres reproduces all three — \( 895/3600 = 0.249 \), \( 895/14\,400 = 0.0622 \), \( 895/40\,000 = 0.0224 \) — which is worth carrying because it needs no unit conversion. The reason 22 mm fails is not the absolute size but the change in it: the sleeve movement available for a 1% speed change is a fraction of a millimetre, which the friction in any real linkage will absorb entirely.

quiz.q:
Sizing a Porter governor

Problem. A Porter governor has 2 kg balls and a 20 kg sleeve weight, with upper and lower arms meeting on the axis. Find the ball height at 200 rev/min and compare it with the Watt governor at the same speed. Then find the sleeve mass needed to give a 150 mm height at 250 rev/min with the same 2 kg balls.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) At 200 rev/min, \( g/\omega^2 = 0.02236\ \mathrm{m} \) from the previous problem, and the loading factor is \( \dfrac{m+M}{m} = \dfrac{2+20}{2} = 11 \).

(2) \( h = 11(0.02236) = 0.2460\ \mathrm{m} \), against the Watt governor's 0.0224 m — eleven times as much, which is the factor itself.

(3) At 250 rev/min, \( \omega = 26.18\ \mathrm{rad/s} \) and \( g/\omega^2 = 9.81/685.4 = 0.014313\ \mathrm{m} \).

(4) The required factor is \( 0.150/0.014313 = 10.48 \), so \( \dfrac{2+M}{2} = 10.48 \) and \( M = 2(10.48-1) = 18.96\ \mathrm{kg} \).

Answer: 246 mm at 200 rev/min, eleven times the Watt height; a 18.96 kg sleeve gives 150 mm at 250 rev/min. Sanity check: note that the answer to (2) is exactly the loading factor times the Watt result, because the sleeve load enters as a simple multiplier and nothing else changes. Note also what it costs: the 20 kg sleeve is dead weight that must be accelerated every time the governor responds, which makes a heavily loaded governor slow. That is why high-speed engines use a spring instead — the same multiplying effect with a fraction of the moving mass.

quiz.q:
Gyroscopic couple on a turbine's bearings (with a US customary check)

Problem. A turbine rotor has \( I = 25\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2} \) and runs at 3000 rev/min in a vessel that turns at 0.10 rad/s. Its bearings are 2.0 m apart. Find the gyroscopic couple and the bearing reactions it produces, express the reaction in pounds-force, and state what happens if the vessel turns twice as fast.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( \omega = 2\pi(3000)/60 = 314.16\ \mathrm{rad/s} \).

(2) \( C = I\omega\omega_p = 25(314.16)(0.10) = 785.4\ \mathrm{N\cdot m} \).

(3) A couple carried by two bearings 2.0 m apart is a force pair: \( F = C/L = 785.4/2.0 = 392.7\ \mathrm{N} \), one up and one down.

(4) \( 392.7/4.448 = 88.3\ \mathrm{lbf} \).

(5) The couple is linear in \( \omega_p \), so doubling the turn rate to 0.20 rad/s doubles it to 1570.8 N·m and the bearing reactions to 785.4 N.

Answer: 785.4 N·m, giving \( \pm 392.7 \) N (88.3 lbf) at the bearings, and both double if the vessel turns twice as fast. Sanity check: the load exists only while the vessel is turning and reverses when it turns the other way, so it is a transient, fully reversed duty that no steady-state bearing calculation would ever show. Its direction is worth stating carefully too: the couple acts about the axis perpendicular to both the spin and the precession, so a rotor yawed by the vessel's turn reacts in pitch — it tries to lift one end of the machine, not to resist the turn.

quiz.q: The difference between a flywheel and a governor is that
choices: a flywheel limits fluctuation within a cycle; a governor sets the mean speed
quiz.solution: A flywheel is a passive energy store that smooths the swing within one revolution and has no view about what the average speed should be; if the load falls away it simply speeds up. A governor measures speed and changes the energy supplied, which is a feedback loop. Machines that need both fit both, and confusing them is why a surging engine is sometimes given a bigger flywheel, which cannot help.

quiz.q: In a simple Watt governor, doubling the ball mass
quiz.solution: \( h = g/\omega^2 \) contains no mass at all. The ball mass appears in both the centripetal requirement \( m\omega^2r \) and the weight \( mg \), and cancels when their ratio sets the arm angle. This is why the Watt governor cannot be tuned by changing the balls, and why a sleeve load, which does not cancel, is the standard way to change its behaviour.

quiz.q: A Porter governor's height exceeds the Watt value by the factor
quiz.solution: \( h = \frac{m+M}{m}\cdot\frac{g}{\omega^2} \), so a 2 kg ball with a 20 kg sleeve gives 11, not 10 — the balls' own weight is still being carried. Using \( M/m \) instead is the standard slip and lands about 10% low here, more at small \( M/m \).

quiz.q: An isochronous governor is one that
choices: holds the speed perfectly and is the design goal
moves through its whole sleeve travel with no change in speed, and therefore hunts
quiz.solution: Isochronism is the limiting case of sensitiveness: every sleeve position corresponds to the same speed, so there is no unique equilibrium for the governor to settle at. It drives the sleeve to one extreme, overshoots, and drives it to the other — hunting. It sounds like the ideal and is a fault, which is the same lesson a control engineer learns about excessive proportional gain.

quiz.q: Hunting in a governed engine is cured by
quiz.solution: Hunting is an over-responsive loop, so the fix is to reduce the response and dissipate energy in it — a small deliberate speed range across the sleeve travel, plus friction or a dashpot. Raising the sensitiveness makes it worse. A larger flywheel smooths fluctuation within a cycle and does nothing about an oscillation of the mean speed, which is a different phenomenon on a much longer timescale.

quiz.q: The gyroscopic couple on a rotor is
quiz.solution: \( C = I\omega\omega_p \) — the rate of change of the angular-momentum vector \( I\omega \) as its direction is swung at \( \omega_p \). \( I\omega \) alone is the momentum, and \( \tfrac12 I\omega^2 \) is the kinetic energy the flywheel of Lesson 9 stores; neither is a couple.

quiz.q: A rotor spinning about a fore-and-aft axis is precessed by a vessel turning in yaw. The gyroscopic couple acts
choices: about the spin axis, opposing rotation
about the yaw axis, resisting the turn
about the axis perpendicular to both, in pitch
quiz.solution: The couple is perpendicular to both the spin and the precession, so a rotor yawed by the vessel's turn reacts in pitch — it tries to lift one end of the machine rather than to resist the turn. That perpendicular relationship is what makes gyroscopic effects feel counter-intuitive, and it is why the resulting bearing loads appear where nobody was watching.

quiz.q: Fitting a larger flywheel to a vehicle engine to reduce speed fluctuation also
choices: reduces the gyroscopic couple during cornering
increases the gyroscopic couple during cornering
eliminates the need for a governor
quiz.solution: \( C = I\omega\omega_p \) is proportional to \( I \), so more inertia means a larger couple for the same spin and turn rate — the machine becomes more reluctant to change direction and loads its bearings harder when it does. That is the standing cost of the Lesson 9 decision, and the reason flywheel sizing is bounded from above as well as below.

11.kuwait:
Applied case — the generator set that surged after an overhaul. A governor-controlled engine driving an alternator was overhauled. The governor linkage was cleaned, re-bushed and freed off, and its response was checked and found much crisper than before. In service the set began surging: the speed swung slowly above and below its set point instead of settling, and the electrical output followed it.

Nothing had failed. The overhaul had raised the governor's sensitiveness by removing the friction that had been damping it, pushing it toward the isochronous condition where a whole range of sleeve positions corresponds to one speed. With no unique equilibrium to settle at, the sleeve is driven to one extreme, the engine overshoots, and the sleeve is driven to the other — which is hunting, and it is a property of the loop rather than of any component in it. The engine was not faulty, the governor was not worn, and the linkage was in better condition than it had been for years.

Two practices follow. Friction in a governor linkage is not purely a defect — part of it is the damping the loop needs, so an overhaul that removes it must restore damping deliberately, with a dashpot or a designed speed droop, rather than assume that freer is better. And a machine that surges is telling you about a control loop, not a mechanism: the useful measurement is the speed range across the full sleeve travel, and if that range is near zero the governor is isochronous and will hunt no matter how well it is made.
11.recap:
• A flywheel limits fluctuation within a cycle; a governor sets the mean speed. They are different problems and neither substitutes for the other.
  • A governor is a mechanical feedback loop: the balls' equilibrium is the measurement and the sleeve position is the control action.
  • Watt governor: \( h=g/\omega^2=895/N^2 \) metres. The ball mass cancels completely, so heavier balls change nothing.
  • Height falls as the inverse square of speed — 248.5 mm at 60 rev/min, 62.1 at 120, 22.4 at 200 — and below about 20 mm linkage friction swamps the signal.
  • Porter governor: \( h=\frac{m+M}{m}\cdot\frac{g}{\omega^2} \). A 2 kg ball with a 20 kg sleeve gives a factor of 11 (not 10), restoring 246 mm at 200 rev/min.
  • The dead weight is paid for in response speed, which is why high-speed governors use springs for the same multiplying effect with less moving mass.
  • Sensitiveness is mean speed over speed range; stability requires one radius per speed.
  • Isochronism — full sleeve travel at a single speed — sounds ideal and causes hunting, because there is no unique equilibrium to settle at. Cure with deliberate insensitivity and damping.
  • Gyroscopic couple \( C=I\omega\omega_p \), acting about the axis perpendicular to both spin and precession: a rotor yawed by a turn reacts in pitch.
  • A 25 kg·m² rotor at 3000 rev/min precessed at 0.1 rad/s gives 785 N·m, which is \( \pm393 \) N on bearings 2 m apart — a reversing load that appears only while the machine turns.
  • It scales with \( I \), so the flywheel of Lesson 9 is not free: smoothing a cycle buys gyroscopic couple in every manoeuvre.
